newsitem.title: CHILE: Copper - Chilean copper mines face drought threat.
newsitem.headline: Copper - Chilean copper mines face drought threat.

text.p: A severe drought in central Chile could hurt copper production in coming months at state copper company Codelco's El Teniente mine and Exxon Minerals' Los Bronces pit, said officials.
"We are going through an extremely critical situation," Julio Cifuentes, deputy services manager at El Teniente, said by telephone from the mine.
"It is probable that (the drought) will have an impact on production. We cannot yet estimate it."
El Teniente, south of Santiago, is Chile's third largest copper mine with production of nearly 350,000 tonnes of fine copper a year.

Although the drought -- the worst in the area for 30 years -- has not yet hurt output at El Teniente, the division is taking steps to conserve its water supplies for the critical southern hemisphere summer months, Cifuentes told Reuters.
The mine is spending $1.5 million in projects including improving its water sources high in the Andes and mending leaking pipes, he said.
The three months from January to March will be crucial as the mine relies on snowmelt from the Andes for a large part of its water supplies during this period.
Far less snow than usual fell in the mountains this winter with dams built to store this water practically empty, he said.
"We normally have at least four million cubic metres of water by now in the dams, but this year we have nothing," said Cifuentes.
Concentrate producers like El Teniente and Los Bronces use large amounts of water in the flotation process to separate crushed copper mineral from rock.

Officials at Los Bronces have said proposals being studied by the government to divert water from the Mapocho River could lead to the shutdown of the mine which lies high in the Andes north-east of Santiago.
"Any additional reduction (in water supplies) could mean the halting of mining operations," said Guillermo Garcia, spokesman for Compania Minera Disputada de las Condes which runs the pit.
Closing the mine, which produces 130,000 tonnes of copper a year, would cost Exxon around $300,000 a day, he told La Segunda newspaper.

The situation appears to be less serious at Codelco's Andina division, the other large copper mine in central Chile. Officials have said the division is carrying out projects to maximise its use of its water resources.
Andina, which lies north of Santiago, produces 150,000 tonnes of copper a year.
The drought will raise operating costs at El Teniente as the mine is not able to produce usual amounts of power from its hydro-electric plants, said Cifuentes.

When water levels are normal, El Teniente generates 40 percent of its own energy. But the mine currently only produces 20 percent which means it has to buy in energy from outside producers which is almost ten times as expensive, he said.
Cifuentes estimated that the drought will add one cent a pound to the pit's operating costs.
